question: Just a few weeks after the EU-Mercosur agreement came into force, the Commission decided to suspend imports from Brazil – including beef and poultry – as of 3 September due to shortcomings in the monitoring of the use of antimicrobials.

The problem is particularly serious in the case of beef: the Commission requires proof of compliance with EU standards throughout the animal’s lifetime, and according to experts, full compliance with this condition may not be possible until 2028 or 2029. At the same time, Brazil accounts for around a quarter of the EU’s beef and poultry imports. In this connection: 1.

How can the Commission continue to claim that the EU–Mercosur agreement does not lower standards of protection for European consumers and farmers, when, even after its entry into force, it itself states that the Brazilian monitoring system does not guarantee compliance with EU requirements?
Why did the Commission allow the agreement to enter into force before ascertaining whether or not one of its largest food-exporting partners actually met EU standards?

Will the Commission acknowledge that the case of Brazilian meat demonstrates that European farmers are expected to compete with imports from countries where equivalence of standards exists more in political declarations than in practice?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.11.2026) All products placed on the EU market, whether they are produced domestically or imported, are required to comply with the EU sanitary standards. These requirements are non-negotiable and apply regardless of the third country concerned or trade agreements.

Therefore, the EUMercosur interim Trade Agreement (iTA), as any other agreement between the EU and third countries, has not changed the applicable EU sanitary requirements, including those restricting the use of certain antimicrobials in food-producing animals and products derived from animals intended to be exported to the EU.

Concerning the rules on antimicrobials, the non-inclusion of Brazil in the list of third countries authorised to export to the EU is further evidence of the EU’s unwavering commitment to maintaining its high standards and addressing antimicrobial resistance.

The Commission will continue to ensure that imports comply with the applicable EU requirements, while applying the iTA in accordance with its provisions and without prejudice to the EU’s established level of protection.

In addition, the Vision for Agriculture and Food1 states that the EU will ensure that ambitious EU standards do not lead to economic, environmental and social leakages, and that the European agri-food sector is not put at a competitive disadvantage without corresponding reciprocity.

To ensure that the EU’s concerns about animal welfare and environmental protection are considered, and to uphold EU’s moral values in response to societal demand, the Commission will pursue, in line with international rules, a stronger alignment of production standards applied to imported products, notably on pesticides and animal welfare.
1 Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament, the Council, the European Economic and

Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions: ‘A Vision for Agriculture and Food – Shaping together an attractive farming and agri-food sector for future generations’, 19.2.2025, COM(2025) 75 final.
